claims.evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing experiments using R14E10-GAL4 driving nls-lacZ, showing trh-off cells in the epidermis and trh-on cells in invaginated tubules (Figure 2C-E, G).

claims.claim: A trachealess cis-regulatory module (R15F01) shows both tracheal enhancer activity and silencer activity in the surface epidermal sheet.
claims.source: A trachealess cis-regulatory module that shows both tracheal enhancer activity and silencer activity in the surface epidermal sheet was identified.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reporter assays showing R15F01 drives expression in tracheal cells but not epidermis (Figure 3B', G), and by domain mapping showing both enhancer and silencer elements (Figure 4, Figure 5).

claims.claim: The coupling of trachealess expression with the invaginated structure ensures that only invaginated cells canalize robustly into the tracheal fate.
claims.source: We propose that the coupling of trachealess expression with the invaginated structure ensures that only invaginated cells canalize robustly into the tracheal fate.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observation that Trh expression is maintained only in invaginated cells and that R15F01 activity is restricted to invaginated cells independent of invagination depth.

claims.claim: Ten pairs of tracheal placodes form in the dorsal anterior part of the epidermis in each segment by stage 10.
claims.source: Tracheal morphogenesis is initiated by placode specification; ten pairs of tracheal placodes form in the dorsal anterior part of the epidermis in each segment by stage 10, followed by invagination, branching and fusion (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a description of known tracheal development supported by the schematic in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: trachealess is considered to be a master regulator of tracheal morphogenesis.
claims.source: In this process, the tracheal placodes first appear as a group of cells expressing trachealess (trh), which is considered to be a master regulator of tracheal morphogenesis (Chung et al., 2011; Isaac and Andrew, 1996; Wilk et al., 1996), and then EGF signaling and mitosis synergistically drive invagination by generating centripetal pressure and inducing epithelial sheet buckling, respectively (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013; Nishimura et al., 2007; Ogura et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: EGF signaling and mitosis synergistically drive invagination by generating centripetal pressure and inducing epithelial sheet buckling, respectively.
claims.source: In this process, the tracheal placodes first appear as a group of cells expressing trachealess (trh), which is considered to be a master regulator of tracheal morphogenesis (Chung et al., 2011; Isaac and Andrew, 1996; Wilk et al., 1996), and then EGF signaling and mitosis synergistically drive invagination by generating centripetal pressure and inducing epithelial sheet buckling, respectively (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013; Nishimura et al., 2007; Ogura et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: FGF signaling triggers tracheal branching.
claims.source: Finally, FGF signaling triggers tracheal branching (Figure 1A) (Glazer and Shilo, 1991; Sutherland et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: In trh mutants, apical constriction forming a tracheal pit appears in the center of the placode region, followed by mitosis in the pit cells and rapid, deep invagination.
claims.source: Live imaging of trh1 (an EMS-induced missense allele) mutants at single-cell resolution revealed an unexpected finding: apical constriction forming a tracheal pit appeared in the center of the placode region, followed by mitosis in the pit cells and rapid, deep invagination as seen in the control, although the onset of invagination was delayed (Figure 1B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claims.claim: In trh mutants, the invaginated structure gradually returns to the surface epidermal layer and merges with these cells to form a segmental furrow.
claims.source: Over the next 90 min, the invaginated structure gradually returned to the surface epidermal layer and merged with these cells to form a segmental furrow, leaving no trace of the tracheal structure (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: In trhA14-3/trhB16-11 mutants, would-be tracheal placode cells form a tracheal pit and invaginated structures during stages 11–13.
claims.source: Consistent with this live imaging analysis of trh1, in fixed samples with a heteroallelic combination of TALEN-induced trh null alleles (trhA14-3/trhB16-11, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Kondo et al., 2014), would-be tracheal placode cells labeled with the R14E10 trh primary enhancer (containing the trh66 STAT-responsive element that mediates stage-10 trh expression in the placode (Sotillos et al., 2010), Figure 1D) also formed a tracheal pit (Figure 1E) and formed invaginated structures during stages 11–13 (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fixed sample imaging data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claims.claim: In trhA14-3/trhB16-11 mutants, R14E10-positive cells return to the surface epidermal layer at stage 15.
claims.source: These R14E10-positive cells returned to the surface epidermal layer at stage 15 (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fixed sample imaging data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The appearance of invaginated structures at stage 12 and the disappearance of these structures at stages 15–16 were observed with 100% penetrance.
claims.source: The appearance of invaginated structures at stage 12 and the disappearance of these structures at stages 15–16 were observed, as shown in Figure 1F and G, respectively, with 100% penetrance (stage 12: eight embryos, stage 15–16: ten embryos).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of the phenotype across multiple embryos.

claims.claim: Overexpression of trh by R14E10-GAL4 in trh mutants rescued the phenotype.
claims.source: In addition, the overexpression of trh (trh-OE) by R14E10-GAL4 in the trh mutants rescued the phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: breathless encodes an FGF receptor.
claims.source: One of the Trh target genes is breathless (btl), which encodes an FGF receptor (Ohshiro and Saigo, 1997), and we reported that FGF signaling through Btl is able to trigger invagination independent of EGF signaling and mitotic rounding (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: FGF signaling through Btl is able to trigger invagination independent of EGF signaling and mitotic rounding.
claims.source: One of the Trh target genes is breathless (btl), which encodes an FGF receptor (Ohshiro and Saigo, 1997), and we reported that FGF signaling through Btl is able to trigger invagination independent of EGF signaling and mitotic rounding (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: btl overexpression in trh mutants using R14E10-GAL4 did not rescue tracheal formation from the transiently invaginated tracheal placodes.
claims.source: However, the btl-OE in the trh mutants using R14E10-GAL4 did not rescue tracheal formation from the transiently invaginated tracheal placodes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), indicating that other trh target genes are required to support FGF signaling-triggered tracheal morphogenesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Other trh target genes are required to support FGF signaling-triggered tracheal morphogenesis.
claims.source: However, the btl-OE in the trh mutants using R14E10-GAL4 did not rescue tracheal formation from the transiently invaginated tracheal placodes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), indicating that other trh target genes are required to support FGF signaling-triggered tracheal morphogenesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the failure of btl overexpression to rescue the trh mutant phenotype.

claims.claim: Inhibiting apoptosis by p35 did not prevent the transiently invaginated cells from returning to the epidermis.
claims.source: In addition, inhibiting apoptosis by p35 did not prevent the transiently invaginated cells from returning to the epidermis, indicating that apoptotic cell removal is not the major cause of this anomaly (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Apoptotic cell removal is not the major cause of transiently invaginated cells returning to the epidermis in trh mutants.
claims.source: In addition, inhibiting apoptosis by p35 did not prevent the transiently invaginated cells from returning to the epidermis, indicating that apoptotic cell removal is not the major cause of this anomaly (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the p35 overexpression experiment.

claims.claim: Tracheal formation proceeds by two successive and genetically separable steps: (1) invagination triggered by mechanical forces and (2) maintenance of the invaginated structure controlled by trh.
claims.source: These results demonstrated that trh is essential for maintaining the invaginated structure, whereas it is dispensable for initiating invagination. Thus, tracheal formation proceeds by two successive and genetically separable steps: (1) invagination triggered by the mechanical forces generated through the combined activities of mitosis, EGFR, and FGFR signaling; and (2) maintenance of the invaginated structure controlled by trh.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing trh is dispensable for initiation but essential for maintenance.

claims.claim: Mitosis-triggered invagination was maintained in rho bnl mutants.
claims.source: Since mitosis-triggered invagination was maintained in rho bnl mutants (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013), EGFR and FGFR signaling are dispensable for the maintenance of the invaginated structure.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: EGFR and FGFR signaling are dispensable for the maintenance of the invaginated structure.
claims.source: Since mitosis-triggered invagination was maintained in rho bnl mutants (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013), EGFR and FGFR signaling are dispensable for the maintenance of the invaginated structure.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mitosis-triggered invagination is maintained in rho bnl mutants.

claims.claim: JAK-STAT signaling induces trh expression through a STAT-responsive trh enhancer in the tracheal placodes at stage 10 of embryogenesis before invagination.
claims.source: JAK-STAT signaling induces trh expression through a STAT-responsive trh enhancer in the tracheal placodes at stage 10 of embryogenesis before invagination (Figure 2A) (Brown et al., 2001; Sotillos et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: After invagination, Trh is detected only in all invaginated cells, including the most proximal spiracular branch.
claims.source: After invagination, Trh is detected only in all invaginated cells, including the most proximal spiracular branch (Figure 2C,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C,F.

claims.claim: The number of initial Trh+ cells in the tracheal placode before invagination (stage 10) was 58.2 ± 5.1 (mean ±S.D.) in controls and 67.2 ± 8.5 in the rho bnl mutants.
claims.source: The number of initial Trh+ cells in the tracheal placode before invagination (stage 10) was 58.2 ± 5.1 (mean ±S.D.) in controls and 67.2 ± 8.5 in the rho bnl mutants, respectively, indicating that tracheal fate specification was not compromised in the rho bnl mutants (Figure 2A,B,G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Tracheal fate specification was not compromised in the rho bnl mutants.
claims.source: The number of initial Trh+ cells in the tracheal placode before invagination (stage 10) was 58.2 ± 5.1 (mean ±S.D.) in controls and 67.2 ± 8.5 in the rho bnl mutants, respectively, indicating that tracheal fate specification was not compromised in the rho bnl mutants (Figure 2A,B,G).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar number of initial Trh+ cells in control and rho bnl mutants.

claims.claim: The increase in the number of initial Trh+ cells in the rho bnl placodes reflects the expansion of the tracheal placode due to the earlier role of rho in restricting the size of tracheal placode.
claims.source: The increase in the number of initial Trh+ cells in the rho bnl placodes reflects the expansion of the tracheal placode due to the earlier role of rho in restricting the size of tracheal placode (Raz and Shilo, 1993).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The number of initial R14E10 + cells (57.9 ± 2.7 cells, monitored by using the R14E10-lacZ transgene at stage 10) is almost the same as the number of initial Trh+ cells.
claims.source: The R14E10 fragment contains the trh66 STAT-responsive element that mediates stage9-10 trh expression (Sotillos et al., 2010), and the number of initial R14E10 + cells (57.9 ± 2.7 cells, monitored by using the R14E10-lacZ transgene at stage 10) is almost the same as the number of initial Trh+ cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data.

claims.claim: After cycle-16 mitosis and invagination, the resultant tracheae of the rho bnl mutants were composed of a smaller number of Trh+ cells (trh-on cells, 31.2 ± 6.2 cells) than those of the controls (87.6 ± 6.3 cells).
claims.source: In contrast, after cycle-16 mitosis and invagination, the resultant tracheae of the rho bnl mutants were composed of a smaller number of Trh+ cells (trh-on cells, 31.2 ± 6.2 cells) than those of the controls (87.6 ± 6.3 cells) (Figure 2C,D,G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: In the rho bnl mutants, the number of initial Trh+ cells at stage 10 was reduced at stages 13–14.
claims.source: These findings demonstrate that in the rho bnl mutants, the number of initial Trh+ cells at stage 10 was reduced at stages 13–14.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of initial Trh+ cells and later trh-on cells in rho bnl mutants.

claims.claim: The reduction in Trh+ cells in rho bnl mutants is due to either the disappearance of Trh+ cells from the epithelium or the loss of Trh expression in cells that failed to invaginate.
claims.source: This reduction is due to either the disappearance of Trh+ cells from the epithelium or the loss of Trh expression in cells that failed to invaginate.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about possible mechanisms for the observed reduction.

claims.claim: The R14E10-GAL4-induced nls-lacZ product (β-galactosidase, β-gal) persisted in the initial trh+ cells after termination of R14E10-GAL4 transcription.
claims.source: The R14E10-GAL4-induced nls-lacZ product (β-galactosidase, β-gal) persisted in the initial trh+ cells after termination of R14E10-GAL4 transcription, allowing us to distinguish trh-off (Trh–, LacZ+) and trh-on (Trh+) cells derived from the initial trh-on cell population after invagination (from stage 13 onward).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental strategy for lineage tracing.

claims.claim: In control embryos, there were trh-off cells (31.9 ± 6.7 cells) in the epidermis.
claims.source: Even in control embryos, there were trh-off cells (31.9 ± 6.7 cells) in the epidermis (Figure 2C,G), while all of the trh-on cells were found in the invaginated tubule region (87.6 ± 6.3 cells).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: In control embryos, all of the trh-on cells were found in the invaginated tubule region (87.6 ± 6.3 cells).
claims.source: Even in control embryos, there were trh-off cells (31.9 ± 6.7 cells) in the epidermis (Figure 2C,G), while all of the trh-on cells were found in the invaginated tubule region (87.6 ± 6.3 cells).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: The sum of the trh-on and trh-off cells (119.5 ± 10.5 cells) agreed well with the prediction from the number of initial Trh+ cells (58.2 ± 5.1 cells) and the number of initial R14E10 + cells (57.9 ± 2.7 cells) after one round of cycle-16 mitosis during invagination.
claims.source: The sum of the trh-on and trh-off cells (119.5 ± 10.5 cells) agreed well with the prediction from the number of initial Trh+ cells (58.2 ± 5.1 cells) and the number of initial R14E10 + cells (57.9 ± 2.7 cells, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C) after one round of cycle-16 mitosis during invagination.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell numbers.

claims.claim: 27% of the initial trh+ cells lost their Trh expression, all of which remained in the epidermis.
claims.source: The results showed that 27% of the initial trh+ cells lost their Trh expression, all of which remained in the epidermis.
claims.evidence: This claim is calculated from the quantitative cell counting data.

claims.claim: Many of the trh-off cells remained during the rest of embryogenesis and formed trichomes on their apical surface.
claims.source: Many of the trh-off cells remained during the rest of embryogenesis and formed trichomes on their apical surface (data not shown), suggesting that they adopted the epidermal fate.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on observation of trichome formation.

claims.claim: trh-off cells adopted the epidermal fate.
claims.source: Many of the trh-off cells remained during the rest of embryogenesis and formed trichomes on their apical surface (data not shown), suggesting that they adopted the epidermal fate.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that trh-off cells form trichomes, a characteristic of epidermal cells.

claims.claim: In rho bnl mutants after invagination, the resultant tracheae were composed of 31.2 ± 6.2 trh-on cells and surrounded by 50.4 ± 7.2 epidermal trh-off cells, with a total of 81.6 ± 9.8 cells.
claims.source: After invagination, the resultant tracheae were composed of a smaller number of trh-on cells (31.2 ± 6.2 cells), as mentioned above, and surrounded by an increased number of epidermal trh-off cells (50.4 ± 7.2 cells) than those of the controls, with a total of 81.6 ± 9.8 cells (Figure 2D,G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Blocking apoptosis by p35 in the rho bnl mutants increased the number of both trh-on and trh-off cells.
claims.source: Blocking apoptosis by p35 in the rho bnl mutants increased the number of both trh-on and trh-off cells (Figure 2E,G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: In the rho bnl mutants with or without p35, 62% of the surviving initial trh+ cells remained in the epidermis and lost their trh expression.
claims.source: In the rho bnl mutants with or without p35, 62% of the surviving initial trh+ cells remained in the epidermis and lost their trh expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is calculated from the quantitative cell counting data.

claims.claim: The reduction in trh-on cells in the rho bnl mutants was not simply due to their disappearance from the epithelium.
claims.source: These findings indicated that the reduction in trh-on cells in the rho bnl mutants was not simply due to their disappearance from the epithelium.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that blocking apoptosis increases both trh-on and trh-off cells.

claims.claim: Losses of EGF, FGF, and mitosis in the rho CyclinA (CycA) bnl triple mutant caused a more severe invagination defect.
claims.source: Losses of EGF, FGF, and mitosis in the rho CyclinA (CycA) bnl triple mutant caused a more severe invagination defect (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The initial trh expression at stage 10 was nearly normal even in the rho CycA bnl triple mutant (53.9 ± 7.1 cells).
claims.source: The initial trh expression at stage 10 was nearly normal even in the triple mutant (53.9 ± 7.1 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The number of Trh-on tracheal cells in rho CycA bnl triple mutants was 6.0 ± 2.5 cells.
claims.source: However, although all the invaginated cells were Trh-positive, the number of Trh-on tracheal cells in these triple mutants was much smaller than expected (6.0 ± 2.5 cells, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), which strongly argues against the model in which the tube-forming trh-on cells are predetermined before invagination.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The observation that the number of Trh-on cells in rho CycA bnl triple mutants is much smaller than expected strongly argues against the model in which the tube-forming trh-on cells are predetermined before invagination.
claims.source: However, although all the invaginated cells were Trh-positive, the number of Trh-on tracheal cells in these triple mutants was much smaller than expected (6.0 ± 2.5 cells, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), which strongly argues against the model in which the tube-forming trh-on cells are predetermined before invagination.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the quantitative data.

claims.claim: The trh expression in the stage 10 tracheal placodes is maintained only in the successfully invaginated tubule cells, independent of the depth of invagination.
claims.source: These observations support the possibility that the trh expression in the stage 10 tracheal placodes is maintained only in the successfully invaginated tubule cells, independent of the depth of invagination.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations in various mutants.

claims.claim: The placode cells that failed to invaginate and remained in the epidermis lost their trh expression.
claims.source: The placode cells that failed to invaginate and remained in the epidermis lost their trh expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing experiments showing trh-off cells in the epidermis.

claims.claim: A mechanism exists to maintain trh expression only in the invaginated tubule cells and extinguish it in the superficial epidermal cells.
claims.source: These results imply that a mechanism exists to maintain trh expression only in the invaginated tubule cells and extinguish it in the superficial epidermal cells (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations of differential trh expression in invaginated vs. epidermal cells.

claims.claim: A transcriptional reporter of trh [1-eve-1, a lacZ enhancer trap of trh] elicited reporter β-gal expression that was limited to the invaginated tracheal cells.
claims.source: A transcriptional reporter of trh [1-eve-1, a lacZ enhancer trap of trh (Perrimon et al., 1991; Wilk et al., 1996) elicited reporter β-gal expression that was limited to the invaginated tracheal cells (Figure 3B), suggesting that the epidermal expression of trh is repressed at the level of transcription.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The epidermal expression of trh is repressed at the level of transcription.
claims.source: A transcriptional reporter of trh [1-eve-1, a lacZ enhancer trap of trh (Perrimon et al., 1991; Wilk et al., 1996) elicited reporter β-gal expression that was limited to the invaginated tracheal cells (Figure 3B), suggesting that the epidermal expression of trh is repressed at the level of transcription.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that a transcriptional reporter is limited to tracheal cells.

claims.claim: trh47 and trh66 are primary enhancers that drive reporter expression from the early stage of tracheal development.
claims.source: Among the eight trh upstream regions with phylogenetically conserved STAT-binding sites, trh47 and trh66 drive reporter expression from the early stage of tracheal development, and trh67 is proposed to be a trh-dependent auto-regulatory element (Sotillos et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: trh67 is proposed to be a trh-dependent auto-regulatory element.
claims.source: Among the eight trh upstream regions with phylogenetically conserved STAT-binding sites, trh47 and trh66 drive reporter expression from the early stage of tracheal development, and trh67 is proposed to be a trh-dependent auto-regulatory element (Sotillos et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The two primary enhancers, trh47 and trh66, were active in both tubule cells and the surrounding epidermal cells.
claims.source: We found that the two primary enhancers, trh47 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and trh66 (covered by R14E10, Figure 3A, Figures 1D and 2C), were active in both tubule cells and the surrounding epidermal cells, suggesting that they did not reproduce the epidermal extinction of trh.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and other figures.

claims.claim: trh47 and trh66 did not reproduce the epidermal extinction of trh.
claims.source: We found that the two primary enhancers, trh47 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and trh66 (covered by R14E10, Figure 3A, Figures 1D and 2C), were active in both tubule cells and the surrounding epidermal cells, suggesting that they did not reproduce the epidermal extinction of trh.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that these enhancers are active in both tracheal and epidermal cells.

claims.claim: trh67 did not drive reporter expression in all of the Trh-positive invaginated cells.
claims.source: In contrast, trh67 did not drive reporter expression in all of the Trh-positive invaginated cells, suggesting that additional cis-elements control the tube-specific maintenance of trh expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Additional cis-elements control the tube-specific maintenance of trh expression.
claims.source: In contrast, trh67 did not drive reporter expression in all of the Trh-positive invaginated cells, suggesting that additional cis-elements control the tube-specific maintenance of trh expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the incomplete expression pattern of trh67.

claims.claim: R15F01 showed strict tube-specific activity after invagination, and its activity was maintained in the invaginated tubule cells throughout embryogenesis.
claims.source: R15F01 showed strict tube-specific activity after invagination, and its activity was maintained in the invaginated tubule cells throughout embryogenesis (Figure 3B', G) and in postembryonic stages (not shown), in contrast to trh47 and trh66 (R14E10), which show transient activity only from embryonic stage 10 to 11 (Sotillos et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3B', G.

claims.claim: trh47 and trh66 (R14E10) show transient activity only from embryonic stage 10 to 11.
claims.source: R15F01 showed strict tube-specific activity after invagination, and its activity was maintained in the invaginated tubule cells throughout embryogenesis (Figure 3B', G) and in postembryonic stages (not shown), in contrast to trh47 and trh66 (R14E10), which show transient activity only from embryonic stage 10 to 11 (Sotillos et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: A few epidermal cells sporadically showed leaked R15F01 activity, especially when monitored using R15F01-GAL4 reporter transgenes.
claims.source: We note that a few epidermal cells sporadically showed leaked R15F01 activity, especially when we monitored the activity using R15F01-GAL4 reporter transgenes (Figure 3B').
claims.evidence: This claim is based on observation of reporter expression.

claims.claim: When using a direct lacZ reporter (R15F01-lacZ), R15F01's activity became detectable in part of the tracheal placode before invagination.
claims.source: In addition, when we used a direct lacZ reporter (R15F01-lacZ), R15F01's activity became detectable in part of the tracheal placode before invagination (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G), slightly later than that of the other early enhancers (trh47 or R14E10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claims.claim: R15F01 repressed the function of an adjacent mini-yellow gene in the adult epidermis.
claims.source: In addition, we noticed that R15F01 repressed the function of an adjacent mini-yellow gene (mini-y included in attP40 or attP2, a transgene landing site on chromosome 2L or chromosome 3L, respectively [Groth et al., 2004]) in the adult epidermis (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation of adult fly body color shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The function of the endogenous yellow gene on chromosome X was not affected by R15F01.
claims.source: The function of the endogenous yellow gene on chromosome X was not affected (data not shown), suggesting that R15F01 represses mini-y expression in cis.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on observation.

claims.claim: R15F01 represses mini-y expression in cis.
claims.source: The function of the endogenous yellow gene on chromosome X was not affected (data not shown), suggesting that R15F01 represses mini-y expression in cis.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that endogenous yellow is not affected while mini-y is repressed.

claims.claim: R15F01 is a cis-regulatory module (CRM) that simultaneously functions as an enhancer in tracheal tube cells and a silencer in epidermal sheet cells.
claims.source: These results suggested that R15F01 is a cis-regulatory module (CRM) that simultaneously functions as an enhancer in tracheal tube cells and a silencer in epidermal sheet cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the dual activity of R15F01 in different cell types.

claims.claim: In mutant combinations that prevented invagination to various degrees, no or only a few epidermal cells showed R15F01 activity, while the small tracheal tubes were R15F01-positive irrespective of the depth of invagination.
claims.source: Using the mutant combinations that prevented invagination to various degrees (combinations of rho, bnl and CycA), no or only a few epidermal cells showed R15F01 activity, while the small tracheal tubes were R15F01-positive irrespective of the depth of invagination (Figure 3C,D,H–K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reporter expression data in various mutants shown in Figure 3C,D,H–K.

claims.claim: In the rho bnl mutants, R15F01 activation was detected at stage 10 before invagination.
claims.source: In the rho bnl mutants, R15F01 activation was detected at stage 10 before invagination.

results.result: The master gene trachealess (trh) is dispensable for initiating tracheal invagination but essential for maintaining the invaginated structure. Live imaging and fixed sample analysis of trh mutants show that tracheal placodes can form pits and undergo transient invagination, but these structures return to the surface epidermis by stage 15-16. This demonstrates that tracheal formation proceeds through two genetically separable steps: invagination initiation (trh-independent) and structure maintenance (trh-dependent).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C11-C16 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (live imaging of trh1 mutants, fixed samples of trhA14-3/trhB16-11 null alleles, and rescue experiments) all demonstrating the same phenotype with 100% penetrance. The live imaging data (Figure 1B,C) directly visualizes the transient invagination, while fixed samples confirm the temporal dynamics. The rescue experiment (C16) provides genetic validation. This represents a major revision of previous understanding that trh was required for invagination initiation.

results.result: Initial trh expression occurs in bipotential tracheal/epidermal placode cells, but after invagination, trh expression is maintained only in invaginated cells while being extinguished in cells remaining in the epidermis. Lineage tracing experiments using R14E10-GAL4 driving nls-lacZ show that in control embryos, 27% of initial Trh+ cells lose expression and remain in the epidermis, while all trh-on cells are found in invaginated tubules. In rho bnl mutants with impaired invagination, 62% of initial Trh+ cells remain in the epidermis as trh-off cells.
results.evaluation: The lineage tracing approach (C35-C45) provides robust quantitative evidence with appropriate statistical analysis (Figure 2G shows significant differences with p<0.001). The cell counting data are internally consistent: the sum of trh-on and trh-off cells (119.5±10.5) matches predictions from initial Trh+ cells (58.2±5.1) after one round of mitosis. The p35 apoptosis inhibition experiment (C43) rules out cell death as the primary mechanism. The data strongly support that trh expression maintenance is linked to successful invagination rather than predetermined cell fate.

results.result: Analysis of rho CycA bnl triple mutants, which have severe invagination defects, shows that despite nearly normal initial trh expression at stage 10 (53.9±7.1 cells), only 6.0±2.5 cells maintain Trh expression after invagination. This strongly argues against a model where tube-forming trh-on cells are predetermined before invagination, supporting instead that trh expression maintenance depends on successful invagination independent of invagination depth.
results.evaluation: The triple mutant analysis (C46-C49) provides critical evidence by testing an extreme condition where invagination is severely impaired. The quantitative data show a much greater reduction in trh-on cells than would be predicted if cells were predetermined (expected ~26 cells after mitosis, observed 6.0±2.5). This result is internally consistent with the rho bnl double mutant data and strengthens the conclusion that invagination status, not predetermined fate, determines trh expression maintenance.

results.result: A mechanism exists to maintain trh expression only in invaginated tubule cells while extinguishing it in superficial epidermal cells. The transcriptional reporter 1-eve-1 shows expression limited to invaginated tracheal cells, indicating transcriptional-level repression in the epidermis. The data from various invagination mutants suggest that tissue-geometry-dependent mechanisms are involved in tight coupling of invaginated structures and Trh expression, ensuring that only invaginated cells canalize into the tracheal fate.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 establish transcriptional regulation through the 1-eve-1 reporter data. Claims C138-C142 synthesize the evidence from multiple mutant backgrounds to propose a geometry-dependent mechanism. While the molecular mechanism is not fully elucidated, the evidence from rho bnl vs. rho CycA bnl comparisons (C140-C141) strongly supports the conclusion that cells are not predetermined and that geometry plays a role. The inference is well-supported by the data, though the specific molecular mechanism remains to be determined.

results.result: The R15F01 cis-regulatory module was identified as showing strict tube-specific activity after invagination, with activity maintained throughout embryogenesis. R15F01 functions as both a tracheal enhancer and an epidermal silencer, as demonstrated by its repression of an adjacent mini-yellow gene in adult epidermis (in cis) while driving tracheal expression. Some sporadic leakage to epidermal cells is observed with GAL4 reporters.
results.evaluation: The identification of R15F01 (C61) is supported by reporter expression data showing tube-specific activity (Figure 3B', G). The dual enhancer/silencer function (C68) is supported by multiple lines of evidence: tracheal expression (C61), mini-yellow repression (C65), and the observation that endogenous yellow is unaffected (C66-C67), demonstrating cis-acting silencer activity. The caveat about sporadic leakage (C63) is appropriately noted. This is a key finding enabling subsequent mechanistic studies.

results.result: R15F01 activity is maintained specifically in invaginated cells regardless of invagination depth, and this maintenance is independent of JAK-STAT, EGFR, and FGFR signaling. In various invagination mutants (rho, bnl, CycA combinations), R15F01 is active only in invaginated cells, not in epidermal cells. Initial R15F01 activation involves EGF signaling (reduced but not absent in rho bnl mutants: 39.5±4.7 vs. 47.3±6.1 cells in controls) and is controlled by a multistep mechanism, as the number of initial R15F01+ cells exceeds the final number of trh-on cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C77 provide comprehensive analysis of R15F01 regulation across multiple genetic backgrounds. The quantitative data (C71) show statistically meaningful differences. The upd1-3 triple mutant analysis (C75) definitively demonstrates JAK-STAT independence for maintenance. The multistep mechanism inference (C73-C74) is supported by the numerical discrepancy between initial activation and final maintenance. The conclusion that R15F01 maintenance is geometry-dependent and signaling-independent is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple mutant combinations.

results.result: Trh is involved in but not essential for initial R15F01 activation (29.4±6.7 cells in trh mutants vs. 47.3±6.1 in controls), and some R15F01 activity can be maintained in a trh-independent manner (19.1±6.8 cells at stage 15 in trh mutants). However, Trh overexpression alone is not sufficient to maintain R15F01 activity in non-invaginated cells, as demonstrated by rescue experiments where surface-remaining cells with Trh overexpression (even phosphomimetic active form) do not show R15F01 expression, while all invaginated cells do.
results.evaluation: The quantitative data on R15F01 activation in trh mutants (C78) clearly show reduced but not absent activation. The maintenance data (C80-C81) demonstrate partial trh-independence. The critical experiment (C83-C84) using trh overexpression with R14E10-GAL4 provides strong evidence that Trh is necessary but not sufficient, as invaginated cells show R15F01 activity while surface cells with Trh overexpression do not. This supports the conclusion (C85) that secondary mechanisms associated with invagination are required. The experimental design appropriately tests sufficiency.

results.result: Trh overexpression using R15F01-GAL4 in trh mutants partially rescues tracheal morphogenesis. At stage 15, R15F01-positive cells maintain invaginated structures but show incomplete branching patterns, possibly due to limited numbers of R15F01-positive cells.
results.evaluation: The partial rescue experiment (C86, C88) is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3. The observation of maintained invaginated structures with incomplete branching is consistent with the later onset and/or smaller number of R15F01-active cells compared to R14E10. This result provides functional validation that R15F01 activity is sufficient for structure maintenance but highlights the importance of proper temporal and spatial activation patterns for complete morphogenesis.

results.result: Domain mapping of R15F01 identified two sub-fragments with tracheal enhancer activity: D7, which drives expression in both tracheal placode and invaginated tubules but also shows epidermal expression near the tracheal pit; and D1, which drives sporadic tracheal expression after invagination. No other sub-fragments (D2-D6, D8) showed tracheal enhancer activity. D7 alone is insufficient to reproduce the tube-restricted pattern after invagination.
results.evaluation: The domain mapping experiments (C89-C94) systematically test all sub-fragments with clear results shown in Figure 4. The identification of D7 as a major enhancer (C90) and D1 as a minor/sporadic enhancer (C91) is directly supported by reporter expression data. The negative results for other fragments (C92) are important controls. The observation that D7 shows epidermal activity (C93-C94) is critical for understanding that additional silencer elements are required for proper spatial restriction.

results.result: R15F01 contains multiple redundant silencer elements in at least two regions: one in the D1-D2 fragment (which shows mini-yellow silencer activity) and another in the D3-D6/D8 region (as del4 lacking D1-D2 still shows epidermal suppression). The combination of D1 with D7 in constructs del2 and del3 reproduces the full R15F01 expression pattern. An epidermal silencer that represses D7's epidermal activity must reside outside D7, as D7 alone shows epidermal expression not seen in full-length R15F01.
results.evaluation: The silencer mapping (C95-C102) uses complementary approaches: mini-yellow repression assays and analysis of deletion constructs. The identification of D1-D2 silencer activity (C95-C96) is supported by adult body color data. The evidence for a second silencer region (C101-C102) comes from del4 analysis showing epidermal suppression despite lacking D1-D2. The reconstitution experiments with del2 and del3 (C100) provide functional validation. The logic is sound and the evidence converges on multiple redundant silencers.

results.result: R15F01 silencer elements can act dominantly on heterologous enhancers. Fragments D1-D2, D3-D6, and del1 (D1-D6) all silence the svb E6B epidermal enhancer activity. Since D1-D2 and D3-D6 do not overlap, this confirms that R15F01 contains multiple redundant silencer elements that act dominantly over epidermal enhancers.
results.evaluation: The heterologous enhancer experiments (C103-C105) provide strong evidence for dominant silencer activity. The use of svb E6B, a well-characterized epidermal enhancer, is appropriate. The non-overlapping fragments D1-D2 and D3-D6 both showing silencing activity (C104) definitively demonstrates redundancy. The reporter expression data (Figure 5C,E,F) clearly show reduced epidermal β-gal expression. This result establishes that the silencers are not specific to trh regulation but can act on other enhancers.

results.result: R15F01 silences enhancer activities in surface epidermis but not in internal tubular organs. When 3×UAS-GFP is driven by arm-GAL4, GFP is detected ubiquitously including epidermis and hindgut. However, 3×UAS-R15F01-GFP shows nearly undetectable epidermal expression while hindgut expression remains detectable. The tracheal signal is enhanced, possibly due to tracheal enhancers in R15F01. Control experiments show that hindgut activity requires arm-GAL4.
results.evaluation: The UAS-based silencing assay (C106-C111) provides elegant evidence for tissue-specific silencer activity. The experimental design with appropriate controls (3×UAS-GFP alone, with arm-GAL4, and 3×UAS-R15F01-GFP with arm-GAL4) allows clear interpretation. The differential silencing in epidermis vs. hindgut (C107, C111) is directly visualized in Figure 5G-I. The control showing hindgut activity requires GAL4 (C109-C110) rules out autonomous R15F01 enhancer activity in hindgut. This demonstrates that R15F01 silencing is specific to surface epidermis.

results.result: Overexpression of breathless (btl), which encodes an FGF receptor and is a Trh target gene, does not rescue tracheal formation in trh mutants, indicating that other trh target genes beyond btl are required to support tracheal morphogenesis. Inhibiting apoptosis with p35 does not prevent transiently invaginated cells from returning to the epidermis, indicating apoptotic cell removal is not the major cause of this phenotype.
results.evaluation: The btl overexpression experiment (C19-C20) provides important negative data showing that FGFR signaling alone is insufficient for rescue, despite previous work showing FGF signaling can trigger invagination. This supports the conclusion that multiple Trh targets are required. The p35 experiment (C21-C22) appropriately rules out apoptosis as the mechanism for structure loss. Both experiments are well-controlled and the conclusions are appropriately limited to what the data show.

results.result: EGFR and FGFR signaling are dispensable for maintenance of invaginated structures. Mitosis-triggered invagination is maintained in rho bnl mutants, and even when both EGFR and FGFR signaling are lost, Trh+ cells maintain invaginated structures. The maintenance of invaginated structures is largely dependent on trh in an EGFR and FGFR signaling-independent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 cite previous work (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013) showing maintenance in rho bnl mutants. Claims C123 and C126 extend this with current observations. The logic is sound: if invaginated structures are maintained in rho bnl mutants (lacking both EGFR and FGFR signaling), then these pathways are not required for maintenance. This is consistent with the finding that trh is essential for maintenance (Result 1) and that trh acts independently of these signaling pathways.

results.result: The conversion of epithelial sheet to tube through invagination and the stabilization of invaginated structures are genetically separable steps. Inductive signals like JAK-STAT prime both tracheal differentiation and invagination separately, consistent with the idea that morphogenetic movement and cell differentiation can be uncoupled. Epithelial tissue can assume two alternative stable structures (sheet or tube), and invagination forces include EGF-regulated myosin contraction, FGF-stimulated cell migration, and mitosis-induced tissue instability. Once invaginated by any driving force, tracheal cells robustly maintain the invaginated structure under Trh control.
results.evaluation: This result synthesizes the major findings into a conceptual framework. Claims C112-C114 are well-supported by the experimental data showing trh mutants can initiate but not maintain invagination. Claims C115-C119 integrate current findings with previous literature on invagination mechanisms. The model that epithelial tissue has two stable states (C115) is a reasonable interpretation of the data, though somewhat speculative. The claims about invagination forces (C116-C118) are appropriately cited to previous work. This represents a valid synthesis of the findings.

results.result: In trh mutants, the degree of invagination is reduced compared to controls. This is consistent with previous findings that trh controls EGFR activation propagation but not initial activation in placodes, indicating trh contributes to tracheal invagination through EGFR signaling propagation in part.
results.evaluation: Claim C120 is based on direct observation from live imaging. Claims C121-C122 appropriately cite previous work (Ogura et al., 2018) and make a reasonable connection to the current findings. The reduced invagination depth in trh mutants is consistent with a role in EGFR propagation. However, this is a relatively minor point in the overall story and relies heavily on previous work for the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Tracheal invagination has unique properties compared to canonical tissue-folding processes. Unlike canonical processes driven by apically concentrated myosin, tracheal invagination involves passive apical constriction under centripetal pressure, acceleration through mitotic cell rounding, and lacks apically concentrated myosin. Candidate Trh-downstream effectors include Crossveinless-c (cv-c) and Crumbs (Crb), but both cv-c and crb mutants maintain tubular tracheal geometry, suggesting trh controls epithelial tissue geometry through activation of multiple genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C129 appropriately cite previous literature establishing the unique properties of tracheal invagination and the dispensability of myosin regulatory light chain. Claims C130-C132 discuss candidate effectors but acknowledge that single mutants are insufficient to disrupt geometry, leading to the reasonable conclusion that multiple genes are involved. This is a fair assessment of the current state of knowledge, though it highlights that the downstream effectors remain incompletely characterized.

results.result: F-actin and microtubule organization, rather than apically concentrated myosin, may support maintenance of invaginated structures. Evidence from salivary gland shows that Arp2/3 overexpression causes reversal of invaginated structures, suggesting F-actin organization is important for epithelial structure stability. Trh is known to reorganize microtubule structures, and in dorsal fold formation, the apical microtubule network plays an important role in cell shortening without apical myosin enrichment.
results.evaluation: This result is largely speculative (C137 explicitly states "might synergistically support"). While the individual observations cited (C133-C136) are from published literature and presumably valid, the connection to tracheal invagination maintenance is inferential. No direct experiments in this manuscript test the roles of F-actin or microtubule organization in trh-dependent structure maintenance. The speculation is reasonable given the cited literature, but lacks direct experimental support in the current work.

results.result: R15F01 is activated in part of placode cells before invagination and senses both initial placode activation cues and morphogenetic invagination cues. R15F01 is also a conserved Polycomb response element (PRE) with concentrated ChIP signals for Polycomb factors, especially in the D1 region. The findings suggest R15F01 functions as a developmental enhancer in tracheal cells while operating as a PRE in other cells including epidermis. Counteracting PRE activity in invaginated cells may be the critical step for coupling Trh expression and tubular architecture, and terminal tracheal differentiation may result from relocation from surface epidermis and suppression of epidermal silencer activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C145 about R15F01 sensing dual cues are supported by the temporal expression data. Claims C146-C148 about PRE identity are based on published ChIP data, which is appropriate. However, claims C149-C152 are largely speculative. The proposal that R15F01 functions as an enhancer in tracheal cells but a PRE in epidermal cells (C150) is an interesting hypothesis but lacks direct experimental evidence in this manuscript. The speculation about counteracting PRE activity (C151) and the model of terminal differentiation (C152) are reasonable interpretations but would require additional experiments to validate. These are valuable hypotheses for future work but remain uncertain based on current data.

results.result: Known signaling pathways (JAK-STAT, EGFR, FGFR) are dispensable for maintaining R15F01 activity in invaginated cells. Possible mechanisms for coupling Trh expression with invaginated structures include mechano-transduction pathways sensing epithelial geometry changes or detection of geometrical conversion through changes in local concentration of secreted molecules. Examples from other systems include intestinal epithelium buckling affecting Shh concentration in chicks and lumen formation with FGF accumulation promoting differentiation in zebrafish. Similar canalization mechanisms coupling gene expression, cell fate, and tissue geometry may play fundamental roles in shaping functional organs.
results.evaluation: Claim C153 is well-supported by the experimental data in this manuscript. However, claims C154-C159 are speculative discussions of possible mechanisms without direct experimental evidence. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities ("One possible mechanism...", "Another possibility...") and cite relevant examples from other systems (C157-C158). The speculation is reasonable and well-informed, but the manuscript does not provide experimental evidence for mechano-transduction or secreted molecule gradients in the tracheal system. Claim C159 about generality is highly speculative. These represent important directions for future research but remain uncertain.

results.result: Background information on tracheal development: Ten pairs of tracheal placodes form by stage 10, followed by invagination, branching, and fusion. Trachealess is considered a master regulator of tracheal morphogenesis. EGF signaling and mitosis synergistically drive invagination, and FGF signaling triggers branching. JAK-STAT signaling induces trh expression through STAT-responsive enhancers before invagination. After invagination, Trh is detected in all invaginated cells. Among trh enhancers, trh47 and trh66 are primary enhancers active from early stages, while trh67 is proposed to be a trh-dependent auto-regulatory element.
results.evaluation: These claims (C7-C10, C17-C18, C26-C27, C30, C55-C56, C62, C124-C125) represent established background knowledge appropriately cited to previous literature. They provide necessary context for the current work. Claim C8 about trh being a "master regulator" is challenged by the current findings showing it's dispensable for invagination initiation, which is a key contribution of this paper. The background information is accurately presented and properly attributed.
